content.title: About
content.content: Puri is a traditional Indian bread made from whole wheat flour, water, salt, and sometimes a small amount of oil. The dough is rolled into small circles and deep‑fried in hot oil until golden. Puri has a light, airy interior and a crisp exterior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Puri is often served at breakfast with vegetable curries, chutney, or yogurt.
The dough is typically unleavened, making the preparation quick.
In some Indian regions, whole‑grain flour and spices such as cumin or coriander are added to the dough.
Puri can be made in bite‑size portions or larger ones, depending on regional customs.
Traditionally, puri is fried in a deep, heavy‑bottomed pan, but any deep‑frying skillet works today.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Puri provides steady energy through slowly digestible carbs, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains plant protein
items.content: Wheat flour supplies a modest amount of protein useful for tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat flour contains B1, B2, and B3 vitamins that support metabolic processes.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: When made with whole‑grain flour, puri adds dietary fiber that promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Provides healthy fats
items.content: Frying in a small amount of vegetable oil adds a dose of monounsaturated fats.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Deep‑frying makes puri calorie‑dense; those watching weight should limit portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Puri is made from wheat flour and is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Risk of overeating
items.content: The crunchy texture and aroma can encourage rapid overconsumption.

items.title: Trans fats from reheating
items.content: Repeated reheating in oil may create trans fats, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve puri hot, straight from the oil. Dip them in chutney, yogurt, or sauces, or use them as a base for "puri‑burgers" with vegetables and meat. In some regions they are split and filled with spiced potatoes or legumes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked puri in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 1‑2 days. For longer storage, freeze them in bags and reheat quickly in an oven or skillet before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Raw cantaloupe is a juicy fruit with a green‑orange rind and bright orange flesh. Native to Southern Africa, it is now cultivated in warm regions worldwide. Cantaloupe offers a sweet, mildly fragrant flavor and a soft, tender texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cantaloupe belongs to the Cucurbitaceae family, making it a close relative of cucumbers, zucchini, and pumpkins.
The fruit is composed of more than 90 % water, making it an excellent hydrator in hot weather.
Its orange flesh gets its color from high beta‑carotene levels, a precursor of vitamin A.
Cantaloupe seeds are edible after roasting and are rich in healthy fats.
Ancient cultures used cantaloupe in rituals and as a symbol of fertility.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in cantaloupe converts to vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C provides antioxidant protection and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: High water content helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Heart‑friendly potassium
items.content: Potassium contributes to normal blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to cantaloupe.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Natural sugars give cantaloupe its sweetness; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If grown with conventional methods, pesticide residues may remain on the rind; thorough washing is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cantaloupe is enjoyed fresh, cut into cubes or wedges. It can be added to fruit salads, smoothies, yogurts, and desserts. The rind is typically not eaten, but the peeled fruit can be used in marinades.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole cantaloupe at room temperature for up to 2–3 days. Once cut, place pieces in an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 5 days. Discard if soft spots or off‑odors develop.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken curry is an Indian dish where bite‑size pieces of chicken are simmered in a fragrant sauce made from spices, tomatoes, and either coconut milk or yogurt. The dish balances heat, sweetness, and creaminess, highlighted by the characteristic aroma of turmeric, coriander, cumin and ginger.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: ‘Curry’ is a generic term for many dishes, not a single spice.
Traditional Indian curry often starts with whole spices toasted in oil (the “tadka”).
Turmeric, the key ingredient, gives the sauce its golden hue and has anti‑inflammatory properties.
Regional variations are wide: southern recipes favor coconut milk, while northern versions use cream or yogurt.
Chicken curry gained worldwide popularity through adaptations to local tastes and ingredient availability.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains beneficial spices
items.content: Turmeric, ginger and garlic offer antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory effects.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Coriander and cumin stimulate bile production, aiding digestion.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken supplies niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: The dish contains iron, zinc and magnesium, supporting immunity and nerve function.

items.title: Spice allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to turmeric, cumin or other spices.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Prepared curry often includes added salt; people with hypertension should watch intake.

items.title: Spiciness level
items.content: Very hot versions can irritate the stomach of those with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Chicken safety
items.content: Use fresh chicken and cook it thoroughly to avoid food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot chicken curry with basmati rice, naan, or flatbreads. It can be added to vegetable stews, used as a filling for wraps, or enjoyed as a quick bowl with quinoa.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Cranberry juice 100% is made from ripe cranberries without any added sugar, concentrates, or other fruit blends. The berries are harvested in northern regions where the climate promotes a high antioxidant content. The juice has a bright red color, a characteristic tart‑sweet taste, and a rich aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cranberries are among the most acidic berries, which is why they are often used as a natural preservative.
Cranberry juice is a traditional beverage in New England (USA) and Canada.
High levels of proanthocyanidins in cranberries help prevent bacterial biofilm formation in the urinary tract.
Cranberry vines grow on shrubs up to 1.5 m tall and prefer acidic, peat‑rich soils.
In the 19th century, cranberry juice was used as a remedy for colds and stomach ailments.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cranberry juice contains proanthocyanidins and vitamin C, which help neutralize free radicals and support the immune system.

items.title: Supports urinary tract health
items.content: Proanthocyanidins inhibit bacteria from adhering to bladder walls, reducing the risk of infections.

items.title: May lower cardiovascular risk
items.content: Studies suggest regular consumption can improve lipid profiles and help lower blood pressure.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The acidity stimulates gastric juice production, promoting better digestion.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The juice provides small amounts of B1, B2, and B6, which are involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity may irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Cranberry juice can enhance the effect of anticoagulants such as warfarin; consult a doctor if you take these medications.

items.title: Added sugars in some products
items.content: Some commercial versions contain added sugar; choose 100% pure juice without additives.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may experience an allergic reaction to cranberries.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the juice chilled as a refreshing beverage, use it in smoothies, cocktails, or as a base for sauces and marinades. To reduce tartness, it is often diluted with water or apple juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. After opening, consume within 5–7 days. Avoid freezing, as it can alter flavor and texture.

ham-sandwich-on-white-with-cheese.title: Ham sandwich on white, with cheese

content.title: About
content.content: A ham sandwich on white bread with cheese is a classic quick snack. It consists of two slices of soft white bread, a thin layer of cream cheese, and a slice of cooked ham. The product is popular in cafés, cafeterias, and as a ready‑to‑eat option in stores.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ham and cheese sandwiches appeared in the United States in the early 20th century as a convenient lunch for workers.
White bread in this sandwich is often toasted to add crunch and prevent sogginess from the cheese.
Cream cheese in the US is often simply called "cream cheese", while in other regions it may be referred to as "soft cheese".
The ham used in ready‑made sandwiches is usually smoked and lightly cured for better flavor.
These sandwiches are frequently served with mustard or mayonnaise as a spread.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Ham and cheese provide high‑quality animal protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Cream cheese supplies calcium and phosphorus, which support bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Ham is rich in vitamin B12 and niacin, important for the nervous system and metabolism.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The sandwich offers a quick source of energy from the carbohydrates in the bread and fats in the cheese.

items.title: Probiotics (when using fermented cheese)
items.content: Some cream cheeses contain live cultures that can benefit gut health.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ham and cheese often contain high levels of salt, which can be an issue for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cream cheese and ham contain saturated fats, so intake should be limited for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to dairy proteins may react to cream cheese.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Prepared ham frequently includes nitrites and other preservatives that may be harmful in excess.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: White bread contains gluten, making the sandwich unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich can be eaten cold or lightly warmed in a toaster. Add lettuce, tomato, mustard or mayo if desired. For a healthier version, use whole‑grain bread and low‑fat cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the ready‑made sandwich refrigerated at 0‑4 °C, wrapped in food‑grade film. Consume within 24 hours. For longer storage, freeze it and thaw in the refrigerator before eating.

hot-dog-sandwich-nfs-on-wheat-bread.title: Hot Dog Sandwich, NFS, on Wheat Bread

content.title: About
content.content: A hot‑dog sandwich is a classic fast‑food item consisting of a grilled or boiled sausage placed inside a split wheat bun. The NFS (No Fillings & Sauces) version means no extra sauces or toppings, highlighting the flavor of the sausage and the bread.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first hot‑dog appeared in the United States in the late 19th century and quickly became popular with railway passengers.
Wheat buns used for classic hot‑dogs are usually soft with a slightly crisp crust after a quick toast.
NFS sausages are often made from beef, pork, or a blend, without artificial fillers.
In some countries hot‑dogs are served with sauerkraut, but the NFS version excludes such additions.
International Hot‑Dog Day is celebrated on July 23.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: The sausage provides about 12 g of protein per 100 g, helping maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef and pork sausages are rich in heme iron, which supports oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: A hot‑dog delivers quick calories, useful during periods of high physical activity.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Sausages contain niacin, vitamin B12, and riboflavin, supporting metabolic processes.

items.title: Carbohydrates from bread
items.content: The wheat bun supplies glucose, the brain’s primary energy source.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Sausages are often salty; excess sodium can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Traditional sausages contain saturated fats, which may contribute to cardiovascular disease when consumed frequently.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have allergic reactions to meat proteins or added preservatives.

items.title: Additives and preservatives
items.content: Certain recipes use glutamates or other additives that can cause sensitivity in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hot‑dogs are typically eaten by hand, holding the bun so the sausage stays in place. Optional condiments like mustard, ketchup, or pickles can be added, but they are omitted in the NFS version.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sausages in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C, and keep a prepared sandwich no longer than 2 hours at room temperature. Keep the bread in a sealed bag in a dry place to prevent it from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Kale (Brassica oleracea var. acephala) is a leafy cruciferous vegetable. Fresh leaves are often used in salads, while cooked kale appears in soups, stews, and casseroles. Adding fat (oil or butter) softens the flavor and enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kale is often called a “superfood” because of its dense nutrient profile.
Leafy cabbages, including kale, were cultivated in ancient Rome.
Kale leaves can be green, purple, or variegated depending on the cultivar.
In Japan, kale (kao) is traditionally served pickled as tsukemono.
Kale tolerates cold better than most leafy greens, making it a staple in northern agriculture.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: One cup of cooked kale provides over 1000 % of the daily value for vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Fresh kale contains about 120 mg of vitamin C per 100 g, supporting immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Source of calcium and iron
items.content: Kale offers a good amount of calcium (~150 mg/100 g) and iron (~1.5 mg/100 g), beneficial for bones and blood formation.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids, quercetin, and sulforaphane in kale help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in kale promotes regular bowel movements and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Thyroid considerations
items.content: Kale contains goitrogens that may affect thyroid function when consumed in excess, especially in people with hypothyroidism.

items.title: Food allergies
items.content: Allergic reactions to cruciferous vegetables are rare but possible.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts of raw kale can cause gas and bloating due to its high fiber content.

items.title: Interaction with blood thinners
items.content: Because of its high vitamin K content, kale may reduce the effectiveness of anticoagulant medications.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use fresh leaves in smoothies, salads, and wraps. For cooked kale, lightly sauté or steam with a small amount of oil to improve vitamin absorption. Kale pairs well with garlic, lemon, nuts, and legumes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh kale in the refrigerator in a perforated bag with a slight moisture layer, preferably in the vegetable drawer. Cooked portions keep in an airtight container for 3‑4 days. Frozen kale should be blanched before packaging and stored in freezer‑safe bags.

content.title: About
content.content: Nachos are crispy corn chips topped with melted cheese. They are a popular snack in bars, movie theaters, and home gatherings. The chips are made from corn flour, water and salt, then fried or baked until golden. The cheese layer usually consists of processed cheese, dairy ingredients and spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial nacho kit appeared in the 1940s at the Taco Bell restaurant.
The name “nachos” comes from Miguel Nacho Ochoa, who first served them in 1943 at the Crispitos eatery.
Corn chips are gluten‑free when made from pure corn flour.
Cheese sauce often contains flavor enhancers like paprika, garlic and onion to boost taste.
In the United States more than 1 billion servings of nachos are sold each year.

items.title: Carbohydrate source
items.content: Corn chips provide a quick source of energy through complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: The cheese topping supplies calcium, essential for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Cheese adds both dairy and plant‑based protein that supports tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheese sauce is often enriched with vitamins B2 and B12, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Dietary fiber in corn
items.content: Corn chips contain a modest amount of fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Nachos are frequently salty, which can raise blood pressure when eaten frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese sauce is rich in saturated fats, which may affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: People allergic to dairy proteins should avoid cheese‑topped nachos.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A single serving can contain 300–500 kcal, so portion control is important.

items.title: Gluten in flavorings
items.content: Some seasoning blends may contain trace gluten; those with celiac disease should check labels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve nachos hot, right after preparation, so the cheese stays melted. Eat them as a standalone snack or with salsa, guacamole, or sour‑cream dip. For a healthier option choose whole‑grain chips and low‑fat cheese sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry chips in an airtight container in a cool, dry place to stay crunchy. Cheese sauce should be refrigerated and used within 5 days after opening. Discard any product that develops off‑odors, mold, or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is the whole grain form of rice that retains the bran layer and germ. After cooking it keeps more nutrients than white rice and has a slightly nutty flavor and firm texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice is less processed than white rice, so it contains more fiber, vitamins, and minerals.
It is a good source of magnesium, selenium, and B‑vitamins.
Compared with white rice, brown rice has a lower glycemic index, helping to better control blood sugar levels.
In Japan and China, brown rice has traditionally been part of heart‑healthy diets.
The bran can oxidize over time, so it is best stored in a cool, dry place.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate cholesterol levels.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium aids normal muscle and nerve function and participates in energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B3, and B6 are involved in carbohydrate metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Provides a slower rise in blood glucose compared with white rice.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: The bran contains phenolic compounds that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; soaking the rice before cooking can mitigate this.

items.title: Arsenic in soil
items.content: In some regions brown rice may contain higher arsenic levels; choose reputable sources.

items.title: Long‑term storage
items.content: Bran can become rancid, so keep rice in an airtight container away from heat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Brown rice can be served as a side dish, base for salads, soups, pilafs, and risottos. It is also added to vegetarian patties and energy bars. Rinse before cooking and optionally soak for 30‑60 minutes to improve texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry brown rice in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. For extended storage, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent the bran from going rancid.

taco-or-tostada-salad-with-chicken.title: Taco or Tostada Salad with Chicken

content.title: About
content.content: Taco or tostada salad with chicken is a Mexican‑style dish that combines crunchy tortillas (taco shells or tostada), tender chicken breast, fresh vegetables, beans, corn, and aromatic spices. It is typically served with salsa, guacamole, or sour cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn tortillas have been used in Mexico for over 3,000 years.
Chicken in Mexican cuisine is often marinated in lime, chili and spices for a distinctive flavor.
A tostada is a “fried tortilla,” giving the dish extra crunch.
The salad is traditionally garnished with fresh cilantro and lime wedges.
It is often served as a “bowl,” allowing each person to customize their portion.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Vegetables, beans, and corn add dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken and whole grains contain B6 and niacin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Salsa and guacamole are rich in vitamin C and carotenoids, which combat free radicals.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Using lean chicken breast and minimal oil keeps the dish light.

items.title: Chicken or gluten allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken or to wheat if a flour tortilla is used.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces and seasonings can be high in salt; monitor added sauce amounts.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Tostada shells and added avocado increase calories; adjust portion size for diet plans.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Break the tortilla, layer chicken, then vegetables, beans, and corn. Drizzle with salsa, add a spoonful of guacamole, and sprinkle cilantro. It can also be served as a standalone salad in a bowl.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Keep tortillas separate to maintain crunch.

content.title: About
content.content: Hot tea with milk is a classic beverage made by steeping black tea and adding hot milk. It offers a smooth, creamy flavor that blends the aromatic notes of tea with the gentle sweetness of milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In the United Kingdom the drink is commonly known as "tea with milk" and is often enjoyed during afternoon tea.
In Russia it is frequently called "milk tea" and is popular in winter as a warming drink.
Adding milk reduces the bitterness of black tea, creating a rounder taste profile.
Traditionally milk is poured into the tea after steeping to avoid curdling from excessive heat.
Some cultures use whole milk, while others prefer low‑fat or plant‑based alternatives.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Black tea contains polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Calcium from milk
items.content: Milk is rich in calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Together tea and milk provide B1, B2 and B6 vitamins, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: A warm drink can relax the stomach and ease digestion.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The combination of tea liquid and milk helps maintain the body’s water balance.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience bloating, gas, or diarrhea after consuming milk.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Black tea contains caffeine, which can cause insomnia or rapid heartbeat if consumed in excess.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein can result in skin rashes, swelling, and other reactions.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Adding whole milk increases the drink’s calories, which should be considered in weight‑control diets.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine may amplify the effects of stimulants and reduce the efficacy of sedative medications.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Steep 1‑2 teaspoons of black tea in 200 ml of water at 90‑95 °C for 3‑5 minutes. Warm 50‑100 ml of milk without bringing it to a boil, then pour into the tea and stir. Sweeten with sugar, honey, or spices (cinnamon, cardamom) if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry tea in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Store milk in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C and use within 3‑5 days after opening.
